title: When Care Changes
description: Understanding how your clinical care pathway may change during pregnancy when there are concerns about you or your pēpi (baby).

contentSections.title: Antenatal screening
contentSections.content:
• Antenatal screening: During pregnancy, you will be offered information about various screening tests that may affect you or your pēpi so you can decide whether to take them.

  • First antenatal blood screen: At your first visit with your LMC or GP, you'll be offered a blood test to check your blood group and rhesus factor, haemoglobin (iron), harmful antibodies, rubella immunity, hepatitis B, syphilis, and HIV. If you are rhesus negative, your LMC or GP will explain what this means.

  • Antenatal HIV screening: All pregnant people in New Zealand are offered HIV testing at the same time as the first antenatal blood screen. Treatment can greatly reduce the risk of passing the virus to your pēpi. The test is highly reliable, but occasionally further tests are needed to confirm results. Your LMC or GP will explain the outcome. More information is available in the HIV testing in pregnancy brochure or on the National Screening Unit's website.

  • Screening for Down Syndrome and other conditions: You can choose whether to have screening for Down Syndrome (trisomy 21, the most common condition) as well as rarer conditions such as Edwards Syndrome (trisomy 18) and Patau Syndrome (trisomy 13).
    • First trimester combined screening (under 14 weeks): A blood test plus an ultrasound (measuring nuchal translucency/NT). The blood test is free; the scan may have a fee.
    • Second trimester maternal serum screening (14–20 weeks): A free blood test.

    Your results are usually available within 7–10 days. If there is an increased chance of a condition, you will be referred to a specialist to discuss options, including diagnostic tests.

  • Diagnostic testing: Procedures such as Amniocentesis (tests the amniotic fluid) or Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS, tests the placental tissue) can confirm whether your pēpi has a condition. These tests carry a small risk of miscarriage (1–2 per 200 people), so some people choose not to proceed.

  • Other antenatal blood tests: Around 26–28 weeks, you will be offered an 'Oral Glucose Challenge Test' (also known as a Polycose Test). This test measures how well your body processes sugar and is used to screen for gestational diabetes in mums. If results are high, a glucose tolerance test may follow.

contentSections.title: Receiving care from a specialist
contentSections.content:
If any complications occur during your pregnancy or labour, you may need to choose between publicly funded hospital specialist services or a private specialist. In many areas of New Zealand, only public hospital specialist care is available. If your LMC believes you should see a specialist, they will discuss it with you.

Often, even when specialist care is needed, your LMC continues to provide primary maternity care. However, a full transfer of care to the specialist may be necessary. Before this transfer occurs, you, your LMC, and the specialist will discuss and agree on each person's role, including yours. If your care transfers to hospital specialists during labour, your LMC may still be able to support you, but this is not always possible.
